query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: High-throughput molecular dynamics simulations using a machine-learning calibrated semi-empirical potential framework under constant-pressure temperature ramp conditions can accurately and efficiently determine the melting temperature, latent heat (enthalpy of fusion), entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys in their random solid solution state before melting.
generation.intervention: Implement high-throughput MD simulations with semi-empirical potentials refined by ML training on available experimental data, running temperature ramp simulations under constant pressure.
generation.conditions: Simulations are performed under an NPT ensemble covering temperatures from below to above melting, within compositional ranges typical of high-entropy alloys.
generation.structural_mediator: The atomic-scale configuration and local ordering captured during the MD runs mediate the phase transformation at melting.
generation.mechanism: The calibrated potentials accurately capture interatomic forces and phase transition energetics, allowing MD simulations to replicate the melting process—yielding predicted melting points, latent heats, entropy changes, and volume variations that mirror experimental observations.
generation.predicted_outcome: Simulation outputs will display melting temperatures, latent heat, and volume changes consistent with experimental results (expected to be within a 10–15% error margin), verifying liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across HEAs.
generation.baseline: Standard MD simulations without ML refinement or calibration often show larger discrepancies from experimental melting behaviors and thermodynamic measurements.
generation.boundary: This method is expected to be applicable to HEAs for which sufficient experimental training data exists, and may be less effective for alloys with compositions or behaviors outside the calibrated range.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative accuracy (e.g., within 10–15% error margins) depends on the quality and representativeness of the training data and potential calibration; further experimental validation is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct high-throughput MD simulations using the ML-calibrated semi-empirical potential under constant-pressure temperature ramp conditions for several HEA compositions. Then, perform corresponding experimental measurements using differential thermal analysis (DTA), high-temperature X-ray diffraction, and calorimetry to obtain melting temperatures, latent heat, entropy changes, and volume variations.
measurements: Melting temperature from simulations compared with DTA measurements
Enthalpy and entropy of fusion from simulations compared with calorimetry data
Volume change at melting from simulations compared with density or high-temperature XRD measurements
Liquid-phase structural properties compared with neutron scattering or additional thermodynamic measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simulation predictions deviate by more than approximately 10-15% from the experimental measurements consistently across multiple HEA compositions or fail to capture the characteristic volume jump at melting, the proposed simulation approach is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Recent research in multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) has increasingly focused on the role of short-range order (SRO) on material performance. However, the mechanisms of SRO formation and its precise control remain elusive, limiting the progress of SRO engineering. Here, leveraging advanced additive manufacturing techniques that produce samples with a wide range of cooling rates (up to 107 K s−1) and an enhanced semi-quantitative electron microscopy method, we characterize SRO in three CoCrNi-based face-centered-cubic (FCC) MPEAs. Surprisingly, irrespective of the processing and thermal treatment history, all samples exhibit similar levels of SRO. Atomistic simulations reveal that during solidification, prevalent local chemical order arises in the liquid-solid interface (solidification front) even under the extreme cooling rate of 1011 K s−1. This phenomenon stems from the swift atomic diffusion in the supercooled liquid, which matches or even surpasses the rate of solidification. Therefore, SRO is an inherent characteristic of most FCC MPEAs, insensitive to variations in cooling rates and even annealing treatments typically available in experiments. cited_evidence.text: The present Monte Carlo simulations are implemented, using a lattice model, where the atoms are constrained to reside on a fixed lattice—in the present case, a BCC lattice. This model is based on the experimental knowledge of the AlxCoCrFeNi phases, and represents the only input from experiment. The simulated cooling transformations involve only redistributions of the atomic population, as an approximation to the behavior of real alloys undergoing sublattice ordering and coherent phase separation. This lattice constraint is too restrictive to address all types of HEA transformations, or to provide high-accuracy simulations: it neglects both the possibility of changing the underlying lattice, and also ignores potential vibrational entropy effects associated with small displacements from the average position. However, the lattice-constrained simulations correctly predict the major trends in some well-known HEAs,,, especially in their as-cast forms, and provide a quantitative framework for understanding the tendencies to both short- and long-range chemical ordering. The shortcomings are addressed in the Discussion section below.

The diffraction images were recorded with a Perkin-Elmer XRD 1621 area detector positioned at a distance 1099 mm from the sample. The exposure time was set to 0.1 s to avoid detector saturation; 100 exposures were summed and recorded into a single image used for further processing with GSAS-II software []. The sample to detector distance, detector tilt, and beam center coordinates was calibrated using NIST CeO2 powder standard available at the beamline and with Y2O3 bead prepared by laser melting. The images from area detector were integrated from 1 to 7° 2Θ at 70–120 ° azimuth into diffraction patterns with 1600 points (0.00375 steps in 2Θ) (see Figure S3). Room temperature diffraction images were collected from every bead before and after laser heating. During the processing of diffraction data from the levitator, sample displacement was refined at room temperature from known cell parameters and kept constant during further refinements. Pawley [,] method, as implemented in GSAS-II, was used for refinement of unit cell parameters at high temperatures.

It can be inferred from the whole computational study of TaNbHfZr R-HEA that many of the thermodynamic, microstructural, strengthening, ductility and dislocation related properties can be obtained from the simulations alone. The thermodynamic changes from the initial random solid solution alloy by hybrid MC/MD structure evolution technique indicates that the entropic contribution to the free energy can be almost 40% of the change of enthalpy due to the presence of local chemical clustering. The quasichemical approximation model deployed here can reflect a gradual and smooth change in Gibbs free energy reaching its equilibrium minimum. Due to the MC/MD structure evolution resembling an annealing treatment, the Hf and Zr-rich SRCs form in the expected {1 0 0} habit planes appearing close to the experimental nanoscale superalloy-like morphology even though the structure is made along dislocation glide direction. The dislocation core is wavy in nature due to the rugged local energy landscape in the multi principal element alloy.
